title: The H-Bridge Circuit: Bidirectional Motor Direction Switching
summary: Explore the classic 4-switch H-Bridge topology, bidirectional current reversal, dynamic braking, and critical shoot-through prevention.

steps.title: Reversing the Polarity: The H-Bridge Architecture
steps.markdownContent:
### Beyond One-Way Motion: The Need for Bidirectional Drive

A single transistor switch can turn a motor ON or OFF, but current can only travel through the motor in one direction. That's fine for an electric desk fan, but useless for a mobile robot! A mobile robot must drive forward, reverse out of dead ends, spin in place, and execute precision maneuvers.

How do you reverse a DC motor? By swapping the polarity of its terminals! If terminal A is positive and terminal B is negative, the motor spins clockwise. If you swap them so terminal B is positive and terminal A is negative, the magnetic force (Lorentz Force) pushes in reverse, spinning the shaft counter-clockwise.

```
       +V Power Rail                   +V Power Rail
           │                               │
       ┌───┴───┐                       ┌───┴───┐
     [Q1]     [Q3]                   [Q1]     [Q3]
       │       │                       │       │
       ├──[M]──┤ (Current: A -> B)     ├──[M]──┤ (Current: B -> A)
       │ (CW)  │                       │ (CCW) │
     [Q2]     [Q4]                   [Q2]     [Q4]
       └───┬───┘                       └───┬───┘
           │                               │
          GND                             GND
     FORWARD ROTATION                REVERSE ROTATION
     (Q1 & Q4 CLOSED)                (Q2 & Q3 CLOSED)
```

### The H-Bridge Solution

Manually unplugging and swapping motor wires on a moving robot is impossible. In electronics, the standard solution is an **H-Bridge circuit**—an arrangement of four solid-state switches (transistors or MOSFETs) forming the shape of the letter **H**, with the DC motor bridging the center horizontal bar.

By selectively commanding pairs of switches, an H-Bridge provides complete control over direction, coasting, and rapid dynamic braking!

quickCheck.question: How does an H-bridge reverse the rotational direction of a DC motor?
options: By reversing the polarity of the voltage and direction of current flowing through the motor terminals
By physically spinning the motor stator 180 degrees
By changing the battery voltage from positive to alternating current
quickCheck.explanation: An H-bridge routes current in either direction across the motor windings, reversing the magnetic torque and rotational direction.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Swapping positive and negative across a DC motor reverses the magnetic push on the rotor.

quickCheck.question: What catastrophic condition is known as 'shoot-through' in an H-bridge circuit?
options: When top and bottom switches on the same leg close simultaneously, shorting the power supply directly to ground
When the motor spins so fast the axle flies off
When the microcontroller sends serial data backwards
quickCheck.explanation: Shoot-through occurs when high and low switches on the same side turn on together, creating a direct short circuit across the power rails.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Never open both gates on the same vertical leg at once—it creates a dead short from power straight to ground!

steps.title: The Four Operational States of an H-Bridge
steps.markdownContent:
### The H-Bridge State Matrix & Shoot-Through Protection

An H-Bridge has four controllable switches: Top-Left ($Q_1$), Bottom-Left ($Q_2$), Top-Right ($Q_3$), and Bottom-Right ($Q_4$). These switches produce four distinct operational states:

| Mode | Q1 (Top L) | Q2 (Bot L) | Q3 (Top R) | Q4 (Bot R) | Motor Terminal A | Motor Terminal B | Resulting Behavior |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Forward** | **ON** | OFF | OFF | **ON** | +V (High) | GND (Low) | Current flows L → R; Forward spin |
| **Reverse** | OFF | **ON** | **ON** | OFF | GND (Low) | +V (High) | Current flows R → L; Reverse spin |
| **Coast (Float)** | OFF | OFF | OFF | OFF | Floating | Floating | High impedance; coast to stop by friction |
| **Dynamic Brake** | OFF | **ON** | OFF | **ON** | GND | GND | Terminals shorted to GND; back-EMF stops rotor! |
| **FATAL SHORT** | **ON** | **ON** | Any | Any | **DEAD SHORT** | **DEAD SHORT** | **SHOOT-THROUGH! Transistors vaporize!** |

### Dynamic Braking vs Coasting
- **Coasting (Freewheel):** When all switches open, current stops, but the rotor keeps spinning due to rotational inertia, slowly coming to a halt from mechanical friction.
- **Dynamic Braking:** When both bottom switches ($Q_2$ & $Q_4$) close simultaneously, both motor terminals connect to Ground. As the spinning rotor continues moving through permanent magnets, it acts as a generator, producing Back-EMF. Because the terminals are shorted together, this generated current produces a powerful counter-torque (electromagnetic brake) that halts rotation almost instantly!

### The Shoot-Through Trap (Cross-Conduction)
If $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are closed at the same time, power flows straight from $+V$ to $\text{GND}$ with near-zero resistance ($R \approx 0\,\Omega$). By Ohm's law, hundreds of amps attempt to flow, instantly destroying the switches. Motor control code must always enforce a **dead-time delay** (a brief microsecond pause) where all switches are disabled before changing directions.

interactiveConfig.question: Which switch combination produces forward rotation in a standard 4-switch H-bridge?
options: Top-left switch (Q1) and bottom-right switch (Q4) closed simultaneously
Top-left switch (Q1) and bottom-left switch (Q2) closed simultaneously
interactiveConfig.explanation: Diagonally opposite switches (Q1 and Q4) allow current to flow from the positive supply rail through the motor to ground in the forward direction.

questions.question: Which switch combination produces forward rotation in a standard 4-switch H-bridge?
options: Top-left switch (Q1) and bottom-right switch (Q4) closed simultaneously
Top-left switch (Q1) and bottom-left switch (Q2) closed simultaneously
questions.explanation: Diagonally opposite switches (Q1 and Q4) allow current to flow from the positive supply rail through the motor to ground in the forward direction.

questions.question: How does dynamic braking stop a spinning DC motor faster than coasting?
options: Shorting both motor terminals together forces generated back-EMF to produce counter-torque that rapidly decelerates the rotor
It reverses the battery polarity at 1000 Volts
It releases mechanical brake fluid onto the axle
questions.explanation: Shorting both motor terminals together allows the back-EMF generated by the spinning rotor to recirculate as reverse torque, braking the motor rapidly.

questions.question: Why is a software 'dead-time' delay essential when switching an H-bridge between forward and reverse?
options: It ensures opening transistors fully turn off before closing transistors turn on, preventing shoot-through short circuits
It gives the Arduino time to save sensor logs to flash memory
It prevents the DC motor from running out of electrons
questions.explanation: Transistors require a finite time to switch off. Dead-time delays prevent top and bottom transistors on the same leg from conducting simultaneously.
